name: Mattress (medium-firm)

lead: A medium-firm mattress balances support and cushioning so the spine stays roughly level. People pick it for comfortable sleep, less back pain and the more rested, upright look they connect to that.

Firmness affects how much the body sinks and how the spine is aligned in lying positions. Sleep and back-pain research, including a 2003 randomized trial, has associated medium-firm beds with less chronic low back pain; no study has tested mattress firmness for facial structure, height or other appearance outcomes.

paras: People choose a medium-firm innerspring, foam or hybrid bed and match it to their sleeping position. Wikipedia says firm mattresses are suggested for stomach sleepers and some back sleepers, soft ones for side sleepers, and medium ones for most back sleepers.

A mattress carries little direct risk. Forum users blame soft surfaces that sag under the lower back for back pain, and the sources reviewed do not endorse a very hard surface. Hospital research on pressure injuries uses specialised foam, air and alternating-pressure mattresses rather than home beds.

angle.text: A supportive medium-firm mattress is chosen for less back pain and better sleep, which people connect to a more upright posture and a rested look. Research links it to lower back pain; facial and skeletal effects have not been tested.

lead: A medium-firm mattress is a bed with an intermediate firmness rating, between soft and firm. Mattresses come in innerspring, foam (polyurethane, memory foam, latex), hybrid, air and water types, and no single numeric firmness scale is given in encyclopedic sources.[1] A 2003 trial used the European Committee for Standardization's Hs scale.[1]

Wikipedia reports that a 2003 randomized trial published in The Lancet linked medium-firm mattresses to less chronic low back pain and that a 2015 systematic review found medium-firm, custom-inflated mattresses best for pain and spinal alignment.[1] A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis has examined which mattress type should be chosen to avoid back pain and improve sleep quality.[2]
Looksmaxxing forum users discuss mattress choice in relation to lower-back support and posture.[3][4][5] No clinical studies have examined mattress firmness for appearance.
infobox: Sleep surface (innerspring, foam, latex, hybrid, air)[1]
Back pain and sleep trials; pressure injury trials in hospitals[1][2][6]
Poor foam layers may wear out within a year; innerspring about 10 years; quality latex 20+ years[1]

paras: Wikipedia describes innerspring mattresses (steel coil cores, including pocketed Marshall coils introduced in 1899), foam mattresses of polyurethane, viscoelastic or latex, hybrids combining coil cores with foam comfort layers, and tick, air and water mattresses.[1] Firmness depends on the comfort layers, the support core and how the bed is built.[1]

The oldest known mattress, about 77,000 years old from South Africa, was made of twigs and leaves.[1] Early mattresses used straw, feathers or horsehair, goatskin water bladders were used in Persia by 3600 BCE, and Comfortaire made the first airbed in 1981.[1] Self-adjusting alternating-pressure beds were introduced in the 1990s to reduce bedsores.[1]

Wikipedia reports that medium-firm mattresses were linked to less chronic low back pain in a 2003 Lancet trial, that a 2015 review favoured medium-firm, custom-inflated beds, and that adjustable-firmness beds may help back pain.[1] It also notes that a 2006 study on sleep and back pain, involving 59 people, was funded by the industry-backed Better Sleep Council.[1]

Quality and firmness claims in this area rest on small or heterogeneous studies, and the 2021 review on mattress type, back pain and sleep quality is the main recent synthesis in the sources reviewed.[2]

No studies found testing medium-firm mattresses for looksmaxxing outcomes such as posture-related appearance, facial structure or height. Studies of mattresses in medicine address back pain and sleep quality and, separately, pressure injuries.[1][2]

An overview of systematic reviews reported that constant low-pressure surfaces, alternating-pressure devices and alternative foams reduced pressure injury incidence compared with standard hospital mattresses or foam, though the authors judged the evidence limited or very limited.[6] A Cochrane review has assessed repositioning regimens for preventing pressure injuries, and a UK trial named PRESSURE 2 compared alternating-pressure mattresses with high-specification foam in high-risk patients.[7][8] A further randomized trial examined pressure-relief mattresses and patient comfort.[9]

On looksmax.org, one user complained that a soft mattress caved in at the lower back and caused back pain, and replies suggested a water mattress or a very flat surface and the floor; the user who replied said he currently slept on an orthopedic mattress and planned to switch to the floor.[3] T Nation members describe shopping for medium-firm or firm mattresses after back or hip trouble, with one citing research pointing to medium-firm and another choosing a firm spring mattress with a foam top.[4][5]
No professional or study-based recommendation for floor sleeping or very hard surfaces is documented in the sources reviewed.

lore.intro: Posts about mattresses on looksmaxxing and fitness forums focus on back pain, lower-back support and posture.[3][4][5]
